description: Labelled claims for evaluating the NLI checker. For each question (all taken from metformin_questions.json, so their evidence phrases are known), three claims: 'grounded' = a paraphrase of what the label says; 'contradicted' = a fact or number changed so the label refutes it; 'unsupported' = plausible-sounding but absent from the label (the typical LLM hallucination). Labels were written by the project author from the label text - one annotator, no adjudication.

claims.text: The usual starting dose is 500 mg taken once a day with the evening meal.
The starting dose is 1,000 mg taken twice daily.
The starting dose does not need to be adjusted for body weight.

items.q: What is the maximum daily dose?

claims.text: The dose should not exceed 2,000 mg per day.
The maximum daily dose is 3,000 mg.
The maximum dose was established in a trial of 3,000 patients.

items.q: How quickly can the dose be increased?

claims.text: The dose can be raised by 500 mg every one to two weeks.
The dose can be raised by 1,000 mg every day.
Dose increases should be supervised by a pharmacist.
Metformin must not be used in patients with severe renal impairment.
Metformin is safe for patients with severe renal impairment.
Metformin is contraindicated in patients with asthma.

items.q: What are the symptoms of lactic acidosis?

claims.text: Symptoms of lactic acidosis include malaise, myalgias and abdominal pain.
Lactic acidosis never causes abdominal pain.
Lactic acidosis commonly causes blurred vision.

items.q: How should suspected lactic acidosis be treated?

claims.text: If lactic acidosis is suspected, prompt hemodialysis is recommended.
If lactic acidosis is suspected, metformin treatment should be continued.
Suspected lactic acidosis should be treated with intravenous insulin.

items.q: How often should vitamin B12 be monitored?

claims.text: Vitamin B12 levels should be measured every 2 to 3 years.
Vitamin B12 levels should be measured every week.
Vitamin B12 supplements should be given to all patients.

items.q: What are the most common side effects?

claims.text: Diarrhea and nausea are among the most common adverse reactions.
Diarrhea is a rare side effect of metformin.
Hair loss is one of the most common side effects.
Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established.
The extended-release tablets are proven safe and effective in children.
Children should take the tablets only with milk.
Metformin decreases the amount of glucose produced by the liver.
Metformin works by increasing insulin secretion.
Metformin works by blocking carbohydrate digestion in the stomach.

items.q: How should the tablets be stored?

claims.text: The tablets should be stored at room temperature, between 20 and 25 °C.
The tablets must be stored in a freezer below -10 °C.
The tablets remain stable for five years after the bottle is opened.

items.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking metformin?

claims.text: Patients should avoid drinking a lot of alcohol while taking metformin.
Drinking large amounts of alcohol is recommended while taking metformin.
One glass of red wine per day lowers the risk of side effects.
